text: Running the numbers on a variant of Grover's algorithm you haven't seen worked out yet is the real test of whether you understand the mechanism, not just the recipe. This lab extends the single-marked-item case from last lesson to two marked items — and the result is deliberately counterintuitive.

Four things to take from this: you'll extend the oracle to mark two items instead of one. A verified, exact result shows that more marked items does not simply mean easier or better amplified. The number of Grover iterations has to match the actual number of marked items, not just the search space size. And the right way to reason about this is explicit state-vector math, not intuition alone.

Take the same 2-qubit search space, but mark two items this time — index 1 and index 3. Because both marked indices share the same low-order qubit value, One, a single Z gate on that qubit is enough to flip both of their signs at once — a reminder that an oracle's gate structure depends on which bit pattern the marked items actually share, not just how many there are.

Starting from the uniform superposition, applying this two-item oracle flips the signs on indices 1 and 3. Applying the same diffusion operator from last lesson, verified by explicit matrix computation — the inner product between the uniform state and the oracle's output comes out to exactly zero, because the positive and negative contributions cancel. The final state after diffusion is exactly uniform again — identical to the starting distribution, before any oracle or diffusion was applied at all. One iteration produced zero net amplification on either marked item.

The reason is visible directly in the math: diffusion's effect scales with that inner product, and with exactly half the search space marked, it cancels exactly to zero. This is the concrete lesson underneath the general iteration-count formula, which depends on pi over four times the square root of N over M, where M is the number of marked items — guessing wrong, even by assuming more marked items always means an easier search, can leave you with literally no improvement over guessing randomly. The real fix in practice: compute the iteration count from your actual M and loop that many times, not a fixed count borrowed from a different-sized problem.

That closes out Chapter 4's algorithm implementations. Chapter 5 turns to interoperability — calling Q# from Python, the practical bridge between Q#'s compiler guarantees and Python's ecosystem, starting with lesson 19.
